newsitem.title: CANADA: Quebec region rebuilds one year after floods.
newsitem.headline: Quebec region rebuilds one year after floods.

text.p: One year after deadly flash floods devastated Quebec's Saguenay region, heart of the French-speaking province's separatist movement, the industrial area is riding a reconstruction wave, mainly funded by Canada's federal government.
Mechanical shovels, trucks, asphalt laying machines and engineers have overtaken this territory of 160,000 people 124 miles (200 km) north of Quebec City, the French-speaking province's capital.
One year ago, an average of more than 11 inches (280 mm) of torrential rains fell within 48 hours across the Saguenay, which is twice the size of Switzerland.
Surging rivers wiped out dams, bridges and highways. Dozens of homes were swept away by the raging waters.

Parts of La Baie, Chicoutimi, Jonquiere and other communities were flooded, wreaking C$700 million ($400 million) of destruction. Two children died in La Baie when their home was engulfed by a mudslide, and flooding claimed eight other lives.
Rail lines at Alcan Aluminium Ltd., which operates three big smelters in the region, were washed out. Production at big paper makers like Abitibi-Consolidated Inc. also was hampered.

Today, backed by C$400 million ($292 million) of reconstruction funds, 80 percent from the federal government in Ottawa, this picturesque region of lakes, rivers and fjords is undergoing an economic boom.
More than 5,000 people have been compensated for flood damage, with 600 others getting compensation by October.

The local unemployment rate has fallen to 12.6 percent from 17 percent a year ago. Construction sector revenues are up almost 30 percent. Private investment of more than C$175 million ($128 million) is planned over the next two years.
Boosting spirits further are Canadian and foreign tourists, who are jamming local hotels and overbooking whale watching tours on the Saguenay and St. Lawrence Rivers.
"This is the biggest summer ever in terms of tourists. They are coming from all over the place," said Leon Aubin, whose convenience store was flooded.
Local engineering consultant Christian Gaudreault has booked contracts totaling tens of millions of dollars, but like other local residents, he is critical of the slow pace of reconstruction.
"There are small-town rivalries here and only the groundwork and road repairs have been done," he said.

Lise Roy and her husband Ghislain, both in their 50s, lost their home when the Ha! Ha! River crested its banks, sweeping away several homes in the river basin. The couple now lives in a four-room apartment with 10 other relatives.
"One year later, we are still living in an apartment. It's really unacceptable. We have not been well looked after," she said.
But government officials said the rebuilding effort demonstrated Canadians' willingness to rise above the troubling question of Quebec's independence to help those in need.
Quebec Intergovernmental Affairs Minister Jacques Brassard, whose hometown is in the region, cited the efforts as an example of cooperation among Quebec City, Ottawa and local authorities.

In addition to the federal money, a Red Cross relief fund raised C$30 million ($22 million) for the Saguenay flood victims, much of it from outside the province. A further C$1.5 million ($1.1 million) of that was set aside for victims of spring flooding in the Western Canadian province of Manitoba.
